GENE_SUMMARY: APC (APC regulator of WNT signaling pathway) is a large scaffold protein that forms the β-catenin destruction complex with AXIN, GSK3β, and CK1α, targeting β-catenin for proteasomal degradation. Loss of APC leads to nuclear β-catenin accumulation and constitutive WNT target gene transcription, the initiating driver event in familial and sporadic colorectal cancer.

The androgen receptor (AR) is a nuclear transcription factor that, upon androgen binding, regulates genes involved in male sexual differentiation and prostate cell proliferation and survival. In prostate cancer, AR acts as an oncogenic driver whose signaling persists even under androgen deprivation through amplification, activating mutations, or splice variants.

ARAF (A-Raf proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase) is a member of the RAF kinase family that transduces signals from RAS to MEK1/2 in the MAPK cascade, promoting cell proliferation and differentiation. Activating mutations and fusions involving ARAF are rare but documented oncogenic events in various cancer types.

ATM (ATM serine/threonine kinase) is the primary sensor and transducer of DNA double-strand breaks. Upon activation, ATM phosphorylates CHEK2, p53, BRCA1, and H2AX to coordinate cell cycle checkpoint activation, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Biallelic loss abrogates the DNA damage response, promoting genomic instability.

ATR (ATR serine/threonine kinase) is activated by RPA-coated single-stranded DNA at stalled replication forks and UV damage sites. It signals through CHEK1 to suppress origin firing, stabilize stalled forks, and prevent premature mitotic entry, protecting genomic integrity during S phase.

Beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) is a component of MHC class I molecules, which present intracellular peptides to cytotoxic T lymphocytes for immune surveillance. Loss of B2M abolishes surface MHC-I expression, allowing tumor cells to evade CTL-mediated killing; it is a recurrent immune evasion mechanism in MSI-high tumors treated with checkpoint inhibitors.

BLM (Bloom syndrome RecQ-like helicase) is a RecQ family helicase involved in resolving DNA secondary structures during replication and dissolving double Holliday junctions to suppress sister chromatid exchanges. Germline biallelic mutations cause Bloom syndrome with extreme genomic instability and markedly elevated cancer risk across multiple tumor types.

BRAF (B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase) is a RAF-family kinase that transduces mitogenic signals from activated RAS to MEK1/2, driving ERK pathway activation. The V600E mutation—present in ~50% of melanomas and common in thyroid, colorectal, and other cancers—renders BRAF constitutively active independent of upstream RAS signaling, and confers sensitivity to BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib).

BRCA1 (breast cancer gene 1) encodes a RING-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase scaffold that coordinates homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks by recruiting repair factors and bridging the resection machinery. BRCA1 also regulates transcription and centrosome duplication. Biallelic loss leads to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), genomic instability, and sensitivity to PARP inhibitors and platinum chemotherapy.

BRCA2 (breast cancer gene 2) is essential for homologous recombination, functioning by binding RAD51 and loading it onto resected single-stranded DNA at double-strand break sites to initiate strand invasion and repair. Loss of BRCA2 causes replication fork instability, HRD, and hypersensitivity to PARP inhibitors, platinum agents, and ionizing radiation.

BRIP1 (BRCA1-interacting protein C-terminal helicase 1, also FANCJ) is a DNA helicase that interacts with BRCA1 at DNA double-strand breaks and is required for normal homologous recombination. BRIP1 also unwinds G-quadruplex structures ahead of replication forks. Germline loss causes Fanconi anemia complementation group J and moderate-risk hereditary breast/ovarian cancer predisposition.

CDH1 (E-cadherin) encodes a calcium-dependent epithelial cell-cell adhesion molecule that suppresses cell migration and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Germline truncating variants cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer; somatic loss is a key step in epithelial tumor invasion and metastasis.

CDKN1B (p27/KIP1) is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that restrains CDK2 and CDK4 activity to prevent cell cycle entry from G1 into S phase. Reduced p27 expression through proteolysis, cytoplasmic mislocalization, or loss-of-function mutations is a common event in hormone-receptor positive breast cancer and other solid tumors.

CDKN2B (p15/INK4B) inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 to maintain the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor in its active form, blocking the G1-to-S phase cell cycle transition. Homozygous deletion of the CDKN2A/CDKN2B locus is among the most frequent copy number alterations across cancer types, particularly in glioblastoma, leukemia, and pancreatic cancer.

CDKN2C (p18/INK4C) is a CDK4/CDK6 inhibitor that maintains RB in its hypophosphorylated, active tumor suppressor state. Loss of CDKN2C is observed in multiple myeloma, medulloblastoma, and other cancers, where it cooperates with other cell cycle regulatory defects to drive uncontrolled proliferation.

CHEK2 (checkpoint kinase 2) is a serine/threonine kinase activated by ATM in response to DNA double-strand breaks. It phosphorylates and activates BRCA1, CDC25A/C, and p53 to enforce S-phase and G2/M checkpoints. Germline variants (including the recurrent 1100delC frameshift) confer moderate-risk hereditary breast cancer predisposition; somatic loss impairs the DNA damage response.

CTNNB1 (β-catenin) is a dual-function protein acting as a structural component of adherens junctions and as a transcriptional co-activator in WNT signaling. In the absence of WNT ligand, β-catenin is phosphorylated and degraded; activating mutations in the N-terminal regulatory domain (exon 3) prevent phosphorylation, causing nuclear accumulation and constitutive transcription of WNT target oncogenes including MYC and CCND1.

EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) is a receptor tyrosine kinase that activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and JAK/STAT pathways upon EGF binding. In-frame deletions in exon 19 and the L858R point mutation in exon 21 confer constitutive kinase activity and sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib); EGFR amplification drives glioblastoma.

ERBB2 (HER2/neu) is a member of the EGFR family of receptor tyrosine kinases that lacks a known direct ligand but transactivates other ERBB receptors by heterodimerization, amplifying mitogenic and survival signals. Gene amplification and protein overexpression are major oncogenic drivers in breast, gastric, and lung cancers, conferring sensitivity to trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and TDM-1.

FBXW7 (F-box and WD repeat domain containing 7) is the substrate-recognition component of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes proteasomal degradation of key oncoproteins including cyclin E, c-MYC, c-JUN, NOTCH intracellular domain, and MCL1. Loss of FBXW7 stabilizes these substrates, promoting cell proliferation, survival, and resistance to apoptosis.

FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by FGF ligands that signals through RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways to regulate proliferation, migration, and differentiation. Gene fusions (e.g., FGFR2-BICC1 in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma), activating missense mutations, and amplification are targetable driver events, with FGFR2-specific inhibitors (pemigatinib, futibatinib) approved in biliary tract cancer.

GNAS encodes the Gsα subunit of the stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein that activates adenylyl cyclase to generate cAMP. Hotspot mutations at R201 and Q227 impair intrinsic GTPase activity, leading to constitutive cAMP/PKA signaling. These mutations drive low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms, IPMN of the pancreas, and pituitary adenomas.

IDH1 (isocitrate dehydrogenase 1) catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate in the cytoplasm. Hotspot mutations at R132 confer a neomorphic enzymatic activity, reducing α-KG to the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which competitively inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (TET2, histone demethylases), causing CpG island hypermethylation and epigenetic dysregulation in glioma and AML; targetable with ivosidenib.

IDH2 (isocitrate dehydrogenase 2) catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α-KG in the mitochondria. Hotspot mutations at R140 and R172 produce the oncometabolite 2-HG, inducing a CpG island methylator phenotype and blocking hematopoietic differentiation. IDH2 R140Q and R172K are targeted by enasidenib in relapsed/refractory AML.

KIT (KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase, CD117) is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor (SCF) that activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and JAK/STAT pathways to regulate hematopoiesis, mast cell development, and gut pacemaker cell maintenance. Activating mutations in the juxtamembrane domain (exon 11, e.g., W557_K558del) or kinase domain drive constitutive signaling in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), systemic mastocytosis, and AML; targetable with imatinib/sunitinib.

KRAS is a small membrane-associated GTPase that transmits signals from activated receptor tyrosine kinases to RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT effectors. Activating mutations at codons G12 (G12C, G12D, G12V), G13, and Q61 impair GTP hydrolysis, locking KRAS in a constitutively active state; KRAS is mutated in ~25% of all cancers. KRAS G12C is specifically targetable with sotorasib and adagrasib.

MAP2K1 (MEK1) is a dual-specificity kinase that phosphorylates and activates ERK1/2, the terminal effector kinase of the RAS/MAPK cascade. Activating missense mutations confer constitutive ERK signaling independent of upstream RAS/RAF activity and are found in low-grade gliomas, melanoma, histiocytic neoplasms, and non-small cell lung cancer; sensitivity to MEK inhibitors (trametinib, cobimetinib) is context-dependent.

Menin (MEN1) is a scaffold protein that interacts with the MLL1/MLL4 histone H3K4 methyltransferase complexes and with multiple transcription factors to regulate gene expression. MEN1 also suppresses JunD-mediated transcription and regulates cell cycle progression. Germline mutations cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1; somatic biallelic inactivation is a major driver in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs).

mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase) is a serine/threonine kinase that forms two complexes (mTORC1 and mTORC2) integrating nutrient, energy, growth factor, and stress signals to regulate protein synthesis, cell growth, autophagy, and metabolism. Activating mutations and pathway amplification (via PIK3CA, PTEN loss) drive proliferation across numerous cancer types; mTORC1 is targeted by rapalogs (everolimus, temsirolimus).

MLH1 (mutL homolog 1) heterodimerizes with PMS2 to form MutLα, the primary endonuclease that cleaves the newly synthesized DNA strand during mismatch repair to excise mismatches. Germline loss-of-function variants cause Lynch syndrome; somatic biallelic inactivation (commonly by promoter hypermethylation) is the major mechanism driving sporadic MSI-high colorectal, endometrial, and gastric cancers.

MLH3 (mutL homolog 3) interacts with MLH1 to form MutLγ, which participates in mismatch repair and meiotic recombination. Variants in MLH3 are associated with Lynch syndrome and colorectal cancer predisposition, with generally lower penetrance than mutations in MLH1 or MSH2; biallelic loss contributes to MMR deficiency.

MSH2 (mutS homolog 2) forms the MutSα heterodimer with MSH6 (recognizes single-base mismatches) and MutSβ with MSH3 (recognizes larger insertion-deletion loops). MSH2 is the most frequently mutated Lynch syndrome gene; somatic biallelic inactivation produces MSI-high tumors with abundant frameshift neoantigens and high sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

MSH6 (mutS homolog 6) forms the MutSα heterodimer with MSH2 to recognize and bind single-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops. Germline truncating variants confer Lynch syndrome susceptibility, generally with a later age of onset than MLH1/MSH2 mutation carriers; biallelic somatic loss drives MSI-high tumorigenesis and immune checkpoint inhibitor sensitivity.

Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) encodes neurofibromin, a RAS GTPase-activating protein (RAS-GAP) that accelerates hydrolysis of RAS-GTP to the inactive RAS-GDP, maintaining RAS in its off state. Loss of NF1 leads to sustained RAS/MAPK activation and is the causative mutation in neurofibromatosis type 1; somatic NF1 mutations are frequent drivers in melanoma, glioma, and triple-negative breast cancer.

NOTCH3 is a transmembrane receptor activated by Jagged and Delta-like ligands; upon cleavage, the NOTCH3 intracellular domain translocates to the nucleus to regulate target gene transcription controlling cell fate, differentiation, and stem cell maintenance. Gain-of-function mutations drive T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, while context-dependent TSG activity is described in other tumor types.

NRAS (neuroblastoma RAS viral oncogene homolog) is a membrane-bound GTPase that transduces growth factor signals to activate the MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways. Activating mutations at codons 12, 13, and 61 (most commonly Q61K/R) prevent GTP hydrolysis, locking NRAS in a constitutively active state; NRAS mutations are prevalent in melanoma (~20%), AML, and thyroid cancers.

NTRK1 encodes TrkA, the high-affinity receptor tyrosine kinase for nerve growth factor (NGF). Oncogenic gene fusions creating constitutively active TrkA fusion proteins (e.g., TPM3-NTRK1) are pan-tumor drivers found across >20 cancer types, including pediatric fibrosarcoma, papillary thyroid cancer, and lung cancer; confers histology-agnostic sensitivity to TRK inhibitors larotrectinib and entrectinib.

NTRK3 encodes TrkC, the receptor tyrosine kinase for neurotrophin-3 (NT-3). Gene fusions producing constitutively active TrkC kinase domains (ETV6-NTRK3 is the archetypal fusion in secretory breast carcinoma) are pan-tumor oncogenic drivers; NTRK3 fusions are biomarkers for TRK inhibitor therapy (larotrectinib, entrectinib) regardless of histology.

NTHL1 (nth-like DNA glycosylase 1) encodes a bifunctional DNA glycosylase/AP lyase involved in base excision repair of oxidatively damaged bases, including thymine glycol, 5-hydroxycytosine, and 5-hydroxyuracil. Germline biallelic NTHL1 variants cause a constitutional base-excision repair deficiency syndrome predisposing to adenomatous polyposis and multiple cancers.

PALB2 (partner and localizer of BRCA2, also FANCN) serves as a bridging protein between BRCA1 and BRCA2 at DNA damage sites, facilitating BRCA2-mediated RAD51 loading and homologous recombination repair. Germline monoallelic loss-of-function variants confer substantially elevated breast and pancreatic cancer risk; biallelic variants cause Fanconi anemia.

PDGFRA (platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha) is a receptor tyrosine kinase for PDGF-A, -B, -C, and -D that activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and STAT5 signaling. Activating mutations (most notably D842V in the kinase activation loop) and gene amplification are driver events in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) and glioblastoma; avapritinib specifically targets PDGFRA D842V.

PDGFRB (platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta) is a receptor tyrosine kinase for PDGF-B and -D that activates proliferative and survival signaling pathways. Chromosomal rearrangements producing fusion proteins (notably ETV6-PDGFRB in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia) and activating point mutations are driver events in hematological malignancies and solid tumors; sensitive to imatinib.

PIK3CA encodes the p110α catalytic subunit of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) that generates PIP3 to activate AKT and mTOR. Hotspot gain-of-function mutations in the helical (E545K, E542K) and kinase (H1047R) domains constitutively activate PI3K signaling and are among the most frequent somatic mutations across solid tumors including breast, colorectal, and endometrial cancers; targetable with alpelisib in PIK3CA-mutated HR+ breast cancer.

PIK3R1 encodes the p85α regulatory subunit of class IA PI3K, which normally maintains the p110 catalytic subunit in a low-activity state. Truncating and certain missense mutations disrupt the p85α inhibitory interface with p110, releasing p110 from negative regulation and constitutively activating PI3K signaling; p85α loss also affects PTEN-PI3K regulatory feedback.

PMS2 (PMS1 homolog 2) heterodimerizes with MLH1 to form MutLα, the strand-discrimination endonuclease that nicks the newly synthesized DNA strand to allow mismatch excision. Germline PMS2 mutations confer Lynch syndrome susceptibility; biallelic constitutional mutations cause constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD) syndrome with childhood cancer predisposition.

POLE encodes the proofreading exonuclease and DNA synthesis catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon. Hotspot exonuclease domain mutations (P286R, V411L) abolish proofreading fidelity, generating an ultramutator phenotype (>100 somatic mutations/Mb) with predominantly C>T transitions in TCA contexts. POLE-mutated tumors are associated with exceptional immunotherapy response due to abundant neoantigens.

POLD1 encodes the proofreading exonuclease catalytic subunit of replicative DNA polymerase delta. Like POLE, exonuclease domain mutations cause an ultramutator phenotype with somatic hypermutation, predisposing to colorectal and endometrial cancers; POLD1-ultramutated tumors may show enhanced immunotherapy response.

PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) is a dual-specificity phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2, directly opposing PI3K activity and negatively regulating the AKT/mTOR survival pathway. PTEN is one of the most frequently inactivated tumor suppressors in human cancer; its loss drives proliferation, survival, and metabolic reprogramming. Cowden syndrome is caused by germline PTEN mutations.

RECQL4 (RecQ-like helicase 4) is a multifunctional helicase involved in DNA replication initiation at origins and stabilization of stalled replication forks during replication stress. Germline loss-of-function variants are associated with Rothmund-Thomson syndrome (poikiloderma, growth retardation, and elevated osteosarcoma risk) as well as RAPADILINO and Baller-Gerold syndromes.

RET (ret proto-oncogene) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase for GDNF family ligands (GFLs) that activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and JAK/STAT signaling to regulate neural crest development and kidney morphogenesis. Activating point mutations (cysteine-substituting extracellular mutations, M918T) drive hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma (MEN2A/2B); somatic RET fusions are oncogenic drivers in papillary thyroid carcinoma and NSCLC, targetable with selpercatinib and pralsetinib.

RNF43 (ring finger protein 43) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation of Frizzled receptors on the cell surface, constituting a negative feedback loop that restrains WNT pathway activation. Truncating mutations in RNF43 prevent Frizzled receptor clearance, leading to WNT pathway hyperactivation and are frequent driver events in colorectal, pancreatic, endometrial, and gastric cancers.

ROS1 is an orphan receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor superfamily with no known endogenous ligand. Chromosomal rearrangements producing ROS1 fusion oncoproteins (e.g., CD74-ROS1 in ~1% of NSCLC) confer constitutive kinase activity and activated RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and STAT3 signaling; ROS1 fusions are pan-tumor biomarkers for crizotinib and entrectinib sensitivity.

SDHA encodes the catalytic flavoprotein subunit of mitochondrial complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) that oxidizes succinate to fumarate in the TCA cycle. Loss-of-function variants impair TCA cycle function, leading to succinate accumulation, which inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (PHD2/3) and stabilizes HIF-1α, driving a pseudohypoxic phenotype in paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma, and gastrointestinal stromal tumors.

SDHD encodes the membrane anchor subunit of mitochondrial complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) that tethers the SDHA-SDHB catalytic core to the inner mitochondrial membrane. Mutations disrupt complex II function, causing succinate accumulation and HIF-1α stabilization; SDHD variants predispose to hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome type 1, with parent-of-origin imprinting (paternal transmission confers risk).

SETD2 is the sole histone methyltransferase responsible for trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 36 (H3K36me3), a mark associated with active transcription, co-transcriptional splicing fidelity, DNA mismatch repair recruitment, and nucleosome displacement. Loss of SETD2 impairs these processes, promoting global splicing alterations, DNA repair defects, and chromatin accessibility changes in clear-cell renal carcinoma and other tumors.

SMAD4 (DPC4) is the common mediator SMAD that forms heterotrimeric complexes with receptor-activated SMADs (R-SMADs) to mediate TGF-β and BMP transcriptional responses, including growth inhibition and differentiation. Loss of SMAD4 abrogates TGF-β-mediated tumor suppression, a critical step in pancreatic adenocarcinoma progression, and is also frequent in colorectal and gallbladder cancers. Germline mutations cause juvenile polyposis syndrome.

SMARCA4 (BRG1) is the ATPase catalytic subunit of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin remodeling complex, which repositions nucleosomes to regulate gene accessibility and expression. Inactivating mutations are the hallmark of SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumors of the thorax (SMARCA4-UT) and rhabdoid tumors, and are also prevalent in NSCLC and ovarian cancer; SMARCA4 loss may sensitize to EZH2 inhibitors.

STK11 (LKB1) is a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates and activates AMPK family kinases, coupling cellular energy status to mTORC1 inhibition, cell polarity establishment, and metabolic homeostasis. Germline STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; somatic inactivation is among the most frequent events in lung adenocarcinoma (~17%), where it promotes immune evasion and resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors.

TP53 (p53) is a sequence-specific transcription factor and master regulator of the cellular stress response that activates DNA repair genes, enforces G1/S and G2/M cell cycle checkpoints, and triggers apoptosis or senescence when damage is irreparable. TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer (~50% of all solid tumors); missense mutations often act as dominant-negatives or acquire oncogenic gain-of-function properties that promote invasion and treatment resistance.

WRN (Werner syndrome RecQ helicase) possesses both DNA helicase and 3'→5' exonuclease activities, resolving aberrant DNA structures at stalled replication forks, Holliday junctions, and telomeres to maintain replication fork stability. Germline biallelic WRN loss causes Werner syndrome with progeroid features and markedly elevated cancer risk; WRN is a synthetic lethal target in MSI-high tumors (WRN inhibitors in clinical development).
